title: What 20 years of NSE data say about Stage 2
data: Weekly stage from the site's engine on NSE prices: every 2nd week from Oct 2006 to Oct 2025, every liquid stock (₹1 Cr+ daily turnover) in Stage 2 — 101,745 snapshots from 1,491 stocks still listed today. Returns are excess over the equal-weight average of liquid stocks for the next year; 'Fell to Stage 4' = the weekly engine showed Stage 4 within the next 26 weeks; 'Worst drop' = median lowest close in the next 6 months.
findings: Late Stage 2 means more risk in both halves of the 20 years: late-phase stocks fell into Stage 4 within 6 months more often (47% vs 34% for early ones in 2007–16, 48% vs 34% in 2017–26), and their median worst drop over the next 6 months was about −15.0% to −16.5% against about −11.5% for early ones.

Lower returns for Late showed up only in 2017–26 (−2.2% a year against the average stock, vs +2.1% for Early); in 2007–16 there was no gap (+2.3% vs +1.3%). Mid did better than Early in both halves (+2.9% vs +1.3% in 2007–16, +4.8% vs +2.1% in 2017–26), so Early's edge is lower risk (34% vs 39% fell into Stage 4), not a higher return. Read Late as 'tighten stops and size down', not 'sell everything'.

The base count was the clearest single sign of maturity: +6.0% a year in the first leg, about +2% after one to three bases, and −1.9% to +0.1% after four or more, with falls into Stage 4 rising from 34% to about 50%.

Time mattered: the edge held for about the first 12 months of the advance (+2.3% to +4.0% a year), then faded (12–24 months: +0.6% and −0.4%, with about half falling into Stage 4) — the same picture as the days-in-Stage-2 test on the RS tab, and close to Weinstein's 'nearly a year'.

Distance above the 150-day line is not a warning: stocks 65–100% above it beat the average stock by +8.5% a year against −1.1% within 5% of it, and fell into Stage 4 far less often (20% vs 64%). More than 100% above the 200-day line kept a good average (+8.5%), but the worst 6-month drop deepened to about −20.0%, so it is shown as a climax warning rather than counted as lateness.

The Stage 2 Score (strength) sorted outcomes in both halves: from −0.9% a year under 40 to +9.0% at 85+, and falls into Stage 4 from 54% to 21%. Best combination: Early with a score of 70+ (+10.2% a year, 49% beat the average stock, 20% fell into Stage 4). Worst: Late with a score under 55 (−2.1%, 60% fell into Stage 4).
caveats: Only stocks still listed today (delisted companies are missing). Snapshots every 2 weeks overlap, so these are averages, not independent trades. Averages are trimmed at the 0.5% tails. The earlier test measured returns against NIFTY 500, which small and mid caps beat over these years, so its numbers were higher. Past results are evidence, not a promise.
rules: Stage 2 = the Stage column (the weekly Weinstein engine) — the same stocks as RS → Stage 2 stocks. The advance starts at the first Stage 2 week after the last Stage 1 or 4; a Stage 3 pause that turns back into Stage 2 stays in the same advance, so the advance can be older than the current Stage 2 run shown on the RS tab. Phase points: base count since the start 0–4 (O'Neil: the base the advance broke out of is the first; a base counts after a 20%+ gain from the last counted pivot; undercutting the previous base's low restarts at 1; two bases = 1 point, three = 2, four = 3, five+ = 4) · months since the advance began 0–2 (6–12 months 1, 12+ months 2) · gain from the low before the start 0–2 (150–300% 1, over 300% 2) · 150-day slope slowing 0–1. Early 0–1, Mid 2–4, Late 5+. Stage 2 Score: RS 25 · 150-day slope 20 · close to the advance's peak 20 · above the 150-day 15 (30–100% best) · above the 50-day 10 · highest close in 6 years 10. Stocks listed too recently for a 150-day line (about 8 months) get no phase.
